Surah al-Isra begins with glorification (tasbih), because the setting is one in which the servant and the Lord are meeting. In such an atmosphere and such circumstances, glorifying and declaring Allah free of imperfection (tahlil) is a fitting act. Here the attribute of servanthood ('ubudiyyah) of Hazrat Muhammad (ﷺ) is mentioned with particular emphasis, because such height and elevation of rank belong to Hazrat Muhammad (ﷺ) precisely as the servant of Allah. Unlike other erroneous religions, which merged the station of servanthood with the station of divinity (uluhiyyah), this distinction must be maintained. The two cannot be combined. For example, after Hazrat Isa (peace be upon him), divinity was ascribed to his person. This was done only because his birth was miraculous, miracles proceeded from him, and then he was raised from this world in a miraculous manner. For these reasons, some people combined the station of divinity and servanthood in the unseen Being. But in this matter, the Islamic creed has been kept simple, clear and pure, and Islam negated every kind of association with the Divine Being, whether close or distant.

Isra' is derived from sara, which means to travel at night. Therefore the meaning of isra' already includes the night, so mentioning the night after isra' is not necessary. Yet in the context of the speech, the night is also explicitly mentioned:

﴿Glory be to He who took His servant by night﴾. This is so that, in depicting this journey, it may be shown that the journey took place under the shadow of night, in a most tranquil environment. It is a distinctive style of the Noble Qur'an that it presents the surroundings of every event beautifully, together with the circumstances in which the event occurs. The same atmosphere settles upon the human faculty of perception and upon the soul, and the person follows the event step by step.

This blessed journey was made by Allah from Masjid al-Haram to Masjid al-Aqsa, and Allah is ﴿Subtle, All-Aware﴾. The purpose and objective of this journey was to show that the source and history of all monotheistic religions and divinely revealed faiths is one. These religions began with Ibrahim and Isma'il (peace be upon them), and their conclusion was with Hazrat Muhammad, Khatam an-Nabiyyin. The sacred places of these religions are likewise equally worthy of respect. Therefore, Khatam an-Nabiyyin is the heir and trustee of all the prophets and their sacred places. Thus this journey is not confined within the limits of time and place; it is not a particular event but a universal journey, and beyond what is understood at first sight, its purpose and objective are far wider, and it contains deep wisdom.

Here, in praise of Masjid al-Aqsa, it is said:

﴿Around which We have blessed﴾. This shows that blessings from Allah continually flow upon this mosque, and it is immersed in them. If it had been said that We made it blessed, or that it contains blessings, the meaning would not have had the same breadth as these words convey: that We blessed its surroundings. This journey was itself a miracle, but within it, further miracles and signs were shown to him.

﴿That We might show him some of Our signs﴾. First of all, the journey from Masjid al-Haram to Masjid al-Aqsa is itself a miracle, for it was completed in so short a time that the Messenger's bed had not yet grown cold. Whatever the manner of that journey may have been, it was nonetheless a miracle. The purpose was to show the Messenger (ﷺ) the wider universe, and to show that great perfections lie hidden within this human lowliness. Moreover, its purpose was to prepare Khatam an-Nabiyyin for the realities that are cast upon the persons of the prophets, and for whose apprehension capacity is given only to those special servants whom Allah has chosen to honour with prophethood. These prophets are from this same human species, which Allah has preferred over a great multitude of His creatures, and within whom Allah has placed most subtle secrets.

﴿Indeed, He is the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing﴾. He keeps every subtle and minute thing in view. He also hears a voice that is very faint; that is, He knows all subtleties and all secrets.

In the context of the speech, the beginning is with the glorification of Allah:

﴿Glory be to He who took His servant by night﴾, and glorifying Allah is praise of Him. After this, the purpose of the journey is stated, which carries an affirmative and definitive aspect:

﴿That We might show him some of Our signs﴾, and after that the discourse again turns to praise of Allah: ﴿Indeed, He is the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing﴾. All these meanings hold a deep balance within themselves. Glorification is an attribute of the Lord, offered from humans to Allah. The purpose is a decision from Allah, and hearing and seeing (Sami' and Basir) are attributes of Allah Himself, expressed in the manner of a statement. In short, all these meanings have been gathered together in one verse with great beauty, and they express their meaning with extreme precision.

The night journey of the Messenger (ﷺ) is a miracle, like the other miracles that Allah has continually made manifest. The miracle lies in that it departs somewhat from the manner of travel to which a human is accustomed. Masjid al-Aqsa has been a stage in this journey. Masjid al-Aqsa is the heart of the region where Allah settled the Children of Israel and from where He later removed them. In the verses that follow, the events concerning the Children of Israel and Hazrat Musa will be mentioned.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 17, verses 2–3:

Exposition: This portion of the history and character of the Children of Israel is mentioned only in this surah of the Holy Quran. It speaks of the end they reached, as a result of which their honour and glory were transformed into decline and misery. Through this historical reflection, people are made to understand how deeply reform and corruption affect the rise and fall of nations. In the subsequent verses of this same surah, the Quran explains that this is the divine sunnah (established way): when Allah wills to destroy a people, He creates corruption among its affluent (mutrafin) ones; they become immersed in deterioration, and are destroyed and thus wiped out.

Here they are told that Musa (peace be upon him) and the Children of Israel were given the Torah. In it there were guidance for them. Then there was their forefather Nuh (peace be upon him), who was ʿabd (a servant of Allah), shakur (grateful) and salih (righteous), and those ancestors who sailed with him in the ark. All these people were righteous and believers, because they had carried righteous believers in the ark with them.

"And We gave Musa the Book and made it a guidance for the Children of Israel, [saying]: Take not other than Me as a Disposer of affairs (wakil). [You are] descendants of those whom We carried with Nuh. Indeed, he was a grateful servant." (17:2–3)

The reason the Children of Israel were given the Book as a reminder and a warning is that it is Allah's principle that He does not destroy or punish a people until proof has been established against them through messengers, which will also be explained clearly shortly.

This is stated as the first purpose of giving the Book to the Children of Israel through Musa (peace be upon him):

"We made it a guidance for the Children of Israel: Take not other than Me as a Disposer of affairs." (17:2) That is, rely upon Allah alone, turn to Allah alone; this is guidance and this is the true faith. For whoever takes someone other than Allah as a disposer of affairs is neither upon guidance nor a believer.

Addressing them, Allah has said: you are the descendants of those whom We carried with Nuh in the ark, and in the first age of this world these people were the essence of humanity. For they were companions and associates of Nuh, a grateful servant, and they were righteous people. Thus Allah wants to tell the believers that a believer's true lineage is his lineage of faith.

Here the attribute of servanthood ('ubudiyyah) of Nuh (peace be upon him) is mentioned, because this is the true goal of humanity. But besides this there is also a wisdom: since the attribute of servanthood of Muhammad (ﷺ) had been mentioned just before, the attribute of servanthood of another distinguished messenger among the messengers, Nuh (peace be upon him), is also mentioned. This is the particular manner of expression of the Holy Quran, which in every case adopts a distinctive style of address.

In the Book that Allah gave to Musa (peace be upon him), the Children of Israel were clearly told that they would be destroyed because of their corruption. You would fall into corruption and deterioration twice, and twice you would be destroyed, because you would twice provide the causes of destruction. For Allah's sunnah is unalterable: any people who fall into corruption and deterioration are destroyed.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 17, verse 4:

"And We decreed for the Children of Israel in the Scripture: 'You will surely cause corruption on the earth twice, and you will become arrogant with great arrogance.'" (17:4) That is, We had already informed the Children of Israel in Our Book that you would create great corruption twice and would show great insolence. This warning was in fact an advance notice that such and such would happen to you, because Allah had advance knowledge of their future end. This information was merely the result of advance knowledge, and there was no element of compulsion in it. Or it may be that the corruption that arose among them later arose merely because of this advance notice, since how is it possible that Allah would compel someone to corruption?

"Say: Indeed, Allah does not command immorality." (7:28) The real matter is that Allah knows what they were going to do. Whatever is in Allah's knowledge, although humans do not know it, and the veil is lifted only when a person actually does that deed.

This was Allah's decision, and He had also told Musa (peace be upon him) in the Scripture that the Children of Israel would create corruption twice in their history, and thus they would adopt arrogance on the earth. They would gain dominance over Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem). But they would use that dominance as a means of corruption. Those over whom they gained superiority would become lawful to them in terms of their lives and honour, and they would destroy the people.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 17, verse 5:

﴿So when the promise of the first of them came, We sent against you servants of Ours of great might, and they went through the very homes [searching]; and it was a promise fulfilled.﴾ (71:5) "When the first of the two occasions of corruption came, We sent upon you Our servants of great strength, and they entered into your land and spread throughout it. This was a promise that had to be fulfilled." This was their first transgression. These people attained progress and high standing in Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem). Power and authority gathered in their hands, and upon this they began to spread corruption. Allah then imposed upon them another mighty and powerful nation. These people had a firm grip. They declared all the territories lawful for themselves, and they kept attacking morning and evening, plundering whatever came before them. They felt no hesitation or fear in doing whatever they wished.

﴿And it was a promise fulfilled.﴾ (17:5) "This was a promise of Allah that had to be fulfilled," because in Allah's promise and decree there can be no failure, and no decree of Allah can be false.

When the Children of Israel tasted defeat, humiliation and slavery, they turned to Allah, set their affairs right, and were thereby delivered from the punishment that had been imposed upon them. Then, because the conquerors too fell into the same kind of corruption, pride in their own power took hold of them, and they also spread corruption in the earth. So Allah, in accordance with His sunnah (established way), organized those who had been subjugated and made them dominant over those invaders, and now the oppressed among the Children of Israel once again prevailed.

“Then We gave you the return of victory over them, and reinforced you with wealth and sons, and made you greater in number.” (71:6) After this, the same pattern is repeated once more. But before the second part of this prophecy comes to pass and the promise made is fulfilled, Allah here sets out a very important foundational law: the law of requital (qanun-e mukafat-e amal).

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 17, verse 7:

"If you do good, you do good for your own selves; and if you do evil, it is for them." (17:7) This is the fundamental principle of retribution (mukafat-i amal), which applies equally in this world and the Hereafter: that a person is himself the rightful owner and bearer of responsibility for his deeds. All their fruits and consequences belong to him. Action and its recompense are inseparable; the result arises from the action. Therefore man is an accountable and responsible being. If he wishes, he may do good to himself or harm himself, and if he receives the fruit of good or bad deeds, he should not complain.

Having stated this principle of retribution, the address now turns back to the prophecy indicated above.

"So when the promise of the Hereafter came, they were to disfigure your faces, and to enter the Masjid as they had entered it the first time, and to destroy completely whatever they subjugated." (17:7) Here, in the context of the discourse, the details of the Children of Israel's second corruption are not given, because it had already been said: "You will certainly cause corruption on earth twice" (17:4). The manner in which the enemies were set over them the second time also shows that they too took the path of corruption the second time.

"So when the promise of the Hereafter came, they were to disfigure your faces" (17:7). That is, the enemies took such revenge upon them that their personality was changed by its effects, to the point that this humiliation and misery appeared on their faces. They dishonored all sacred things and reduced everything to ruin.

"And they would enter the Masjid as they had entered it the first time" (17:7). They entered in the same way the earlier enemies had entered; wherever they gained dominance, they plundered and laid waste to everything they came upon.

"And to destroy completely whatever they subjugated" (17:7). That is, they utterly destroyed Bayt al-Maqdis and, by expelling its people from the land, turned the region upside down.

Thus this prophecy proved true. God's promise was fulfilled, and such people were set over the Children of Israel. Then again enemies were set over them, and they expelled them from the land and ruined the country.

The Qur'an did not specify who these people were, because the purpose of describing the second destruction of the Children of Israel was fully achieved by this much description. Had it been stated that such and such nations were set over them, no additional meaning would have been added. The aim here was to describe the divine law (sunnat-i Ilahi) concerning the rise and fall of nations.

Here a question arises: why does God bring such destructions? It is explained that at times the destruction of a people is itself a cause of mercy for them.

**Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 17, verse 8:**

"It may be that your Lord will have mercy upon you" (71:8). This applies if you take a lesson from your history.

But remember: if you repeat this act of rebellion, its consequences will appear again. The sunnah (established way) of Allah is continuous and unchanging. It does not undergo any alteration.

"But if you return, We too shall return" (71:8). "If you return to your former conduct, We too shall return to Our punishment." Indeed, they committed corruption again, and Allah gave the Muslims power over them and expelled them from the Arabian Peninsula (Jazirat al-Arab). After this, they spread corruption throughout the world, so Allah gave power over them to others among His servants, and Hitler punished them. In the present age, they have again begun corruption and rebellion. Organized in the form of Israel, they have plunged the entire Middle East into calamities. Therefore, it is necessary that Allah set over them a people who will give them the full punishment for their rebellion, so that Allah's promise may be fulfilled, and Allah's promise is always fulfilled. For it is certain that if you do this again, We will do so again. And the time is not far when the Children of Israel will taste the result of their deeds.

Now the context of the discourse turns to the otherworldly end of the disbelievers, because most of the time the disbelievers are the ones who share a common character among themselves.

"And We have made Hell a prison for the disbelievers" (17:8). "This Hell will so encompass them that none of them will be able to escape from it. This Hell will be so vast that all will be contained within it."

In this part of the lesson, the aspect of the history of the Children of Israel that has been described is this: Allah gave the Book to Musa so that these people would take guidance from it. But they did not accept guidance; rather, they went astray, and the destruction of Allah overtook them. Now the context shifts to the Holy Qur'an, that in the same way this Qur'an is also presenting most firm teachings.

This Qur'an guides to the path that is most upright. It is the wellspring of every kind of guidance and the source of guidance for everyone, without any limits or restrictions. Whatever guidance and whatever system humanity needs for its direction is contained in it, in every age and in every kind of society.

To the human conscience and understanding it gives a clear belief and pure, simple ideas, beliefs and conceptions free of any complexity. These ideas cleanse human understanding of illusion, conjecture, superstition and myth, and bring its thinking into harmony with the laws of nature and the fitrah.

Then this Qur'an connects the outer and inner being of a person. It makes human thought and action alike, and creates harmony between human beliefs and deeds. As it were, all aspects of a person's personality are tied together in one thread; the deeds and thoughts of a human being on earth are connected with the higher world; and the struggle a person undertakes in this world becomes worship.

Even in matters of worship its policy and guidance are extremely balanced. It commands only that amount of worship and servitude which is within a person's capacity. It does not give commands such that a person has no power to carry them out. Nor does it abandon a person to laziness and self-indulgence so that he becomes a pleasure-seeker; rather, its instructions in every field are based on balance and moderation.

It also gives extremely firm guidance regarding the mutual relations of human beings: concerning the relationship between individual and individual, between husband and wife, between ruler and ruled, and between nations and governments. This Book establishes all such relations on extremely firm foundations, foundations that are not affected by opinions and desires. Friendship and enmity do not influence these principles, nor do interests and advantages affect these relations. It also knows what comprehensive guidance is suitable for every kind of land and every region. Thus it has set down in this Book a comprehensive system which gives firm guidance for the legal, economic, social and moral needs of all the people of the world, and it has also given excellent international guidance.

It has also given excellent guidance concerning all the revealed religions (adyan samawi), and it has taught the respect due to the sacred places of all religions. Therefore, when a person takes guidance from this Book, the result is that a brotherhood is established among all human beings and people live in great peace and security.

The truth is that this Qur'an shows the path which is straight and firm.

In the preceding verses there were several miraculous indications: the Prophet ﷺ's journey of Mi'raj (Ascension) and the miracles contained within it; the miraculous escape of Hazrat Nuh (Noah) (peace be upon him) from the flood and the reference to those who were with him in the ark; the ebb and flow of the history of the Children of Israel and the miraculous decisions of God among them; and the principle of the rise and fall of nations; and the reference to the recompense of deeds in human life and to the Qur'an being a book of guidance and a method of action.

After all these miraculous matters, the address now turns back to the miracles of the universe. The earlier miracles occurred through the prophets, but these miracles are such that they invite everyone to observe them. Human life's struggle and human deeds are also linked with these cosmic miracles. The result of human deeds and struggle is connected with these laws of nature. Just as the principle of human action and the recompense of deeds flows through the universe, so too the principles of the laws of nature are bound up with human life. Just as human life is based on certain rules, so too this universe is based on certain rules, and there is no deviation within it. This system of night and day, just as it is based on most unchanging rules, so too the Sunnah of God (sunnat Ilahiyyah, the divine way/custom) runs through this universe, and its principles too are unchanging. And they too are moving by the will of that same Divine Being by whose will the night and day are moving.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 17, verse 12:

The laws of nature that govern night and day are bound up with human effort and struggle. The reckoning of years is based on night and day, and human action and conduct are likewise connected with them. Whether a person does good or evil, reward and punishment will follow. Guidance and misguidance are also linked with this. And in all matters the principle of individual responsibility prevails: no bearer of burdens bears the burden of another. Upon this it is also established that Allah does not punish anyone until He has sent a Messenger. And from this it is also connected that when Allah destroys a town, He does so when its affluent (mutrafin) in that situation spread immorality (fisq and fujur) and turmoil and corruption. Upon this principle is also founded that some people seek only the world, and some are seekers of the Hereafter; so Allah gives the people of the world the world, and gives the people of the Hereafter the Hereafter. All these matters, whether religious and social or cosmic, proceed in accordance with one and the same divine law (namus-i-ilahi) which Allah has put into operation in this universe. This divine law and this established sunnah are immutable. No change occurs in its principles. Nothing in it is merely accidental.

﴿And We made the night and the day two signs. Then We effaced the sign of the night and made the sign of the day to give sight, that you may seek bounty from your Lord and that you may know the number of years and the reckoning. And everything We have detailed with full explanation.﴾ (17:12)

Night and day are the greatest signs of this universe, and the system of night and day is based on an extremely precise and subtle principle. It is a process in which no disturbance has ever occurred, and in which there has never been any interruption; night and day continue to move without cease. The question is what is meant by (فمحونا, "then We effaced"). The meaning appears to be that at night there is no light, and the movements and sights of this universe are not clearly visible. Compared with the activities and variety of the day, it can be said that the night is effaced and without light. The day is open, in which everything is seen, while the night is somewhat obscured, in that not everything is seen as in the day. The night was made obscured for this reason, and the day was made open for this reason, that

﴿that you may seek bounty from your Lord and that you may know the number of years and the reckoning﴾ (17:12). The night is a time of rest, tranquility and union, and the day is for struggle, earning and livelihood, and travel; and because of the succession of night and day, the reckoning of years and months is completed. The reckoning of the appointed time, the reckoning of seasons and harvests, in short the reckoning of all affairs, is established by the night and day and their system.

﴿And We have detailed everything with full explanation﴾ (17:12). That is, in this universe nothing, whether important or unimportant, has been left by Us to chance and accident; rather it is in accordance with Our divine law. Or the law of nature is fully detailed, comprehensive and precise; for instance, consider the rotation of night and day alone. This is proof of the profound planning of the Designer of this universe.

Just as a complete order prevails in the universe, so too the principle of recompense for deeds, the law of retribution, is a most profound and immutable order.

"And We have fastened every person's omen to his neck, and on the Day of Resurrection We shall bring out for him a record which he will find laid open. (It will be said:) 'Read your record. Today you are sufficient as your own reckoner.' (71: 31-41)"

A person's omen (ṭā'ir) is his deed, which is written in his destiny. It means the person's own earning and action. Fastening it to his neck means that a person's omen, that is, his deeds, never separate from him. This is the Qur'an's manner: it presents abstract meanings in a concrete, embodied form. The meaning is that every person is responsible for the consequences of his deeds and cannot escape their effects. Likewise, the "open book" on the Day of Judgment also means the manifestation of a person's deeds: the deeds will be laid bare, and none will be able to hide them, nor will any deed be left out of the reckoning. But the Qur'an presents this as an embodied open book, which has a greater impact on the listener and makes the matter part of human feeling. Thus the human mind immediately turns to the bird and the book, and begins to contemplate that harsh Day when all secrets will be exposed. It will be an open book, and on that day no reckoner will be needed.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 17, verse 14:

"Read your record. Your own soul suffices as a reckoner against you this day." (71:41) [sic: the verse reference as given in the source]

This immutable law of divine nature is linked with the law of action and its consequences (mukafat-e-amal).

"Whoever is guided is only guided for his own soul, and whoever goes astray goes astray only to its detriment, and no bearer of burdens shall bear the burden of another." (71:51) Whoever adopts the right path, his rectitude benefits himself alone, and whoever goes astray, the consequence of his error falls upon himself alone. Accordingly, responsibility for deeds is individual, and because of this every person is bound to his own self. If he takes the path of guidance, he does so for himself; if he goes astray, he himself bears the responsibility. No one will be answerable for another's deeds, and no one will be able to lighten another's burden. Every person will be called to account for his own deeds, and only the reward of his good deeds will be given, and no friend will be responsible for another friend.

Out of His great mercy, Allah did not make man accountable and responsible merely by the principle that exists in this natural universe, nor merely by the Covenant of Alast, which Allah took from all human beings when they were in the loins of Adam. Rather, out of great mercy, Allah established a continuous succession of Messengers, who continually reminded people of the sanctity of the Shariah and warned people of the evil end, and He established this principle.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 17, verse 15:

﴿And We would never punish until We have sent a messenger﴾ (71 : 51) "And We are not going to punish until We send a Messenger." It is a great mercy of Allah that before punishing people, He establishes proof against them and leaves them no excuse.

This divine practice (Sunnat Ilahiyyah, the established way of Allah) also applies to the sending of punishment upon people in this world. This punishment too descends in accordance with Allah's law (nāmūs) and leaves no excuse.

This divine practice also applies to the sending of punishment upon people in this world. This punishment too descends in accordance with that law of Allah's power (nāmūs-e-qudrat) according to which the system of night and day continues to operate.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 17, verse 16:

وَإِذَا أَرَدْنَا أَنْ نُهْلِكَ قَرْيَةً أَمَرْنَا مُتْرَفِيهَا فَفَسَقُوا فِيهَا فَحَقَّ عَلَيْهَا الْقَوْلُ فَدَمَّرْنَاهَا تَدْمِيرًا (17:16) "When We intend to destroy a town, We command its affluent ones, and they commit abominations therein; then the word becomes due against it, and We destroy it utterly."

Who are these mutrafin? They are the class of the great ones who are wealthy and live in comfort. Servants stand before and behind them. They seek ease, and prosperity, honour and leadership are theirs. These people become slack, corrupt, and immersed in immorality and debauchery. They set aside lofty values, religious sanctities and dignity, and they become immersed in sensual indulgence and vice. When such people see that there is no one to take their hand, they spread corruption on the earth. Then they spread obscenity and deviance throughout the entire nation. And these people openly trample the lofty values because of which nations are formed and attain ascendancy in the world. In this way, the collective system of the nation becomes loose, and from it the elements of life, strength and progress are gradually removed. Eventually that nation is destroyed and reduced to nothing.

This verse discusses that Sunnah of Allah: when Allah decides to destroy a nation, because it has itself completed all the causes of its own ruin, the mutrafin in it increase. Then Allah loosens the rope of such people, and there is no one to take their hand. These mutrafin become the leaders of the nation, immorality and debauchery become common, and thus the collective system of the nation becomes loose. Slackness enters it, the decision for its destruction is made, and suddenly it is destroyed and ruined. The responsibility for this destruction then rests upon the entire nation, because no one among the individuals of the nation, nor any of its groups, took hold of the hands of the mutrafin. No collective effort and struggle was made for the reform of the system. Therefore there is a need that the mutrafin not be allowed to arise within the nation. Their very existence is a sign that destruction is coming upon the nation. If the collective system of a nation blocks the path of such people and does not let them come into being, the nation can be saved from destruction, because the cause of destruction is only these mutrafin and their corruption and immorality. It is these very people who lead a nation and society towards destruction.

Allah has established for humanity natural laws which are inviolable, and in them there is never any deviation or exception. These are the unchangeable Sunan Ilahiyyah (divine laws of Allah). According to these laws and sunan, when the causes for an event are provided, the event occurs. Thus the will of Allah is fulfilled, the promise of Allah is true, and His word is carried out. But Allah does not command debauchery; He never commands obscenity. Therefore, if a class of mutrafin is found in a society, its very existence is evidence that this society has begun to create the causes of its own destruction. Its joints have become loose, and it is about to be scattered. It is reaching its natural end according to the decree of Divine destiny. What happens is that, according to the decision of the Sunnah of Allah, it is destroyed because of these mutrafin, since it itself allowed this class of mutrafin to come into being.

Now, what is meant here by the will of Allah? It does not mean that Allah seizes people and creates the mutrafin, who then are compelled to commit debauchery, and Allah forcibly causes someone to produce the causes of their own destruction. Rather, in reality, the society itself provides the causes, and according to the Sunan Ilahiyyah the result follows afterwards. It is true that this law of nature and Sunnah of Allah has been established by Allah. But the real cause of destruction is the existence of the mutrafin and debauchery.

From this it is understood that it is an obligation upon society to remove the defect found in the collective system within it, and to prevent the mutrafin from committing debauchery, so that according to the Sunan Ilahiyyah the punishment of destruction and ruin does not come upon the whole society.

From the earliest ages, after Hadrat Nuh (peace be upon him), this Sunnah has been in operation. Age after age has passed, and this has continued to happen. Whenever debauchery became widespread in a nation, that nation was destroyed. And Allah is thoroughly aware of the evil deeds of His servants.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 17, verse 17:

﴿And how many generations have We destroyed after Noah! And sufficient is your Lord as Knower and Seer of the sins of His servants.﴾ (17:17)

Now, at the end, it is explained that some people live only for this world. Only for this world. They do not raise their eyes upward from this earth. Allah provides such people only with the provisions of this world, and in the Hereafter, only Hell falls to their share. Those who live solely for this world, and whose eyes do not search for any vision beyond it, become immersed in this very world. They are steeped in the mud of this earth, lie in filthy drains like worms, and are drowned in every kind of base pursuit of pleasure, becoming slaves of lust and passion. In seeking worldly pleasure, they commit such deeds as cast them into Hell.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 17, verse 18:

﴿Whoever desires the hasty (fleeting) life, We hasten for him therein what We will, for whom We intend. Then We have made Hell for him; he will burn in it, blameworthy and rejected from mercy.﴾ (71:81)

Blameworthy because this is the gain he sought, and rejected from mercy because he has fallen into punishment.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (*Fi Zilal al-Quran*, Urdu translation) on Surah 17, verse 19:

"And whoever desires the Hereafter and strives for it as it should be striven for, while he is a believer, those are the ones whose striving will be appreciated" (71:91). "Whoever desires the Hereafter, and strives for it with the striving due to it, and is a believer, the striving of such a person will be appreciated."

Therefore, those who desire the Hereafter must also strive for it. They must discharge its obligations and fulfil its requirements. All this striving must come after faith. It is clear that faith is not merely a wish or a desire. Rather, faith means that it settles in the heart and that righteous deeds attest to it.

It is correct here that by striving for the Hereafter, a person is not suddenly deprived of the worldly benefits, comforts and pleasures. Rather, while living in this world, he keeps the Hereafter in view. It is not that the world becomes his ultimate aim. The Hereafter is also before his eyes, and when the Hereafter is before a person, then the worldly way of life does not harm him.

As for the person who desires only the world, he will be thrown into Hell, blameworthy and deprived of mercy. And the person who strives for the Hereafter will be received in the Highest Assembly (*Mala' A'la*) with great honour and respect, because he left the world and worked for the Hereafter, and leaving what is near, he raised his gaze to what is distant and to the lofty horizons.

What is the reality of the life of this world? Those who study the lives of insects, creeping creatures, animals and beasts know its reality well. There is no fundamental distinction between the human life of this world and the life of the creeping creatures mentioned above. The life worthy of human beings in keeping with their humanity is the life of the Hereafter. It is an everlasting life in the presence of Allah. Because Allah created man in a special manner, fashioned him in due proportion, breathed into him His special spirit, settled him upon the earth, established him there, favoured him with knowledge, and gave him superiority over the angels.

For the one who strives for the world, the field is also open before him, and for the one who strives for the Hereafter, the field is also open. Allah brings both to their desired aims, objectives and goals. Whether someone wants the world or the Hereafter, Allah does not block anyone's path. Wherever one wishes, the will of Allah carries him there.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 17, verse 20:

"To these and to those, We extend the gifts of your Lord; and the gift of your Lord is never withheld" (17:20).

Yet within this earth, in this world too, differences of rank and degree among people are observed: in their means, in their resources, in their causes, in their inclinations and tendencies, and in the difference of rank according to their striving and effort. For the sphere of this world is also limited, and this globe of the earth is also limited. But in comparison, the Hereafter is vast; its expanses are boundless. The world to come! What can be said of it? In comparison with it, this entire world is not even equal to the wing of a mosquito.

"But look: how We have given some of them preference over others in this world! And in the Hereafter their ranks will be even greater, and their preference will be even greater still."

Therefore, if anyone truly desires an elevated station, he should strive for that great and true distinction which will be in the Hereafter, whose arena is vast and where there is no narrowness or shortage anywhere. And it is so vast that only Allah knows its limits. Those who wish to compete for a position of distinction should compete for the station of the Hereafter. Why should one run after the lowly and meager provisions of this base world!

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 17, verse 22:

In the first lesson of this surah, the principles of action and its recompense, the laws of guidance and misguidance, and the responsibilities of earning and accountability were linked to cosmic principles, natural laws, and the alternation of night and day. In this lesson, human conduct, morals and manners, individual ethics, and collective behaviour and laws are linked to the fundamental principles and beliefs of the Islamic outlook on life, namely the Oneness of God (Tawhid al-Ilahi). Thus, the foundation of all individual and collective relationships is this belief in Tawhid, which is a strong rope. And this alone is the foundation and bond of the collective life of a family and a society.

In the previous lesson it was said that this Qur'an gives direct guidance to the straightest path, and that all the details of this guidance are recorded within it.

﴿Indeed, this Qur'an guides to that which is most upright and gives good tidings to the believers who do righteous deeds that they will have a great reward. And [it warns] that those who do not believe in the Hereafter, We have prepared for them a painful punishment.﴾ ﴿Man prays for evil as he prays for good, and man is ever hasty.﴾ ﴿And We made the night and the day two signs. We effaced the sign of the night and made the sign of the day visible, that you may seek bounty from your Lord and that you may know the number of years and the reckoning. And everything We have explained in detail.﴾ (17:9–12)

Whereas in this lesson, some of the commandments of the Qur'an, and some of its prohibitions, are given in detail, and these relate to the practical affairs of human life.

Thus the lesson begins with the prohibition of shirk, and it is declared that Allah alone, without partner, is worthy of worship. After this, the commandments begin. The first command concerns good treatment of parents. Then come good treatment of relatives, the needy and travellers; moderation and safeguarding in giving and spending; fulfilment of covenants; the command to keep weights and measures balanced; the command to remain firm on truthfulness; avoidance of arrogance; and finally, again, avoidance of shirk. Thus all moral and legal commandments are bound within the belief in Tawhid, because the entire Islamic system rests upon the Islamic outlook on life, and the Islamic outlook on life rests upon the pure word (Kalimah Tayyibah).

In this verse, a prohibition of shirk is given and a warning of its evil consequence is issued. The command is general, but by putting it in the singular form, an individual is addressed, so that every individual understands that this command is for him, and that it has been issued specifically for each person. Because belief is a personal matter, and in regard to it each person is individually accountable. The consequence is that whoever commits shirk will be censured, because he has committed a blameworthy act. And the second consequence is that he will remain humiliated and without helper or supporter, even though in his own thinking he may have many helpers. And the one who becomes blameworthy and no one comes to his aid, he too withdraws and sits down in shame. Because a person in a state of weakness often sits down; he cannot make any movement. Therefore the word qu'ud (sitting) is most meaningful for such a person in this place.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 17, verse 23:

﴿And your Lord has decreed that you worship none but Him.﴾ After shirk, this command is now given that worship also be only for Allah, and this command is given in the form of a decree. That is, just as a decree is a final matter and its execution is necessary, so too the execution of this command is necessary. By the word qada (decreed), the command is further emphasized. Besides this, negation and exception (la ilaha illa Allah) are in themselves an emphatic and restrictive style, meaning that this alone should be the case and nothing else. Thus, within the style of expression, the method of further emphasis has been adopted, because tawhid in belief (tawhid fi'l-aqidah) and tawhid in worship (tawhid fi'l-ibadah) are extremely fundamental matters.

And when this principle, foundation and basis has been laid down, then individual commands begin to be issued, and collective commands and laws begin to be enacted. Before this, the belief in tawhid has been planted in minds. Through this belief, the impulse toward deeds, obligations and laws has also already arisen within souls.

For a human being, the first bond is belief. It is beliefs and ideologies alone that can keep people united. After beliefs and ideologies, the first unit for humanity is the unit of the family, and the family is formed through parents. Therefore the first command given is that, alongside the worship of Allah alone, you should show good treatment to your parents, and in Islam this has great importance; it is the first value.

﴿And to parents, good treatment...﴾ (42).

With a very beautiful style of speech and very gentle and heart-moving words, the Qur'an creates in the hearts of children respect and honour toward parents, and stirs in their conscience and heart the feelings of tenderness. The reason is that when life proceeds along its paths, everyone's gaze, emotions, concern and attention are directed forward. Every person, instead of turning back toward parents, turns forward toward his own children. Everyone is concerned for the next generation; few are those who look backward. Attention toward father, mother and those who have passed on belongs to few people. Therefore the Qur'an felt the need to awaken in children's conscience and awareness concerning parents and the generation that is passing, so that by looking back they would treat their parents well.

All parents have a natural impulse to worry for their children; parents even give their lives for them. Just as a grain, mixing with the soil, takes on the form of a sprouting plant and itself disappears, and whatever is inside an egg takes the form of a chick, so children take all the juice, all the strength, all the care and all the power from their parents, and parents become frail and old. Often death grants them respite, and they spend their lives in utter helplessness. As for children, they very quickly forget all this and look forward, turning to their own duties. Their attention is toward their own wives and children, and thus the chain of life moves on.

It is a fact that father and mother do not need to be told to take care of their children; rather, children need the instruction to take care of their aged parents, and there is a need to awaken their conscience and awareness in this matter, so that they also look after the welfare of the generation that dried up the last drop of its blood to raise them, until it itself became dry and frail.

The command of good conduct and kindness toward parents was given by Allah in the form of a judgment and decree. That is, it is Allah's decision, and every ruler enforces his decision. The meaning is that this command is extremely emphatic, being in the form of a decree. Just as earlier it was said that Allah has decreed that you worship Him alone.

After this, there is a discourse about parents in a very compassionate, generous and tender manner. In a deeply emotional way, the hardships parents endured during childhood are mentioned, and it is explained how much love and affection they showed to the child.

﴿If one or both of them reach old age with you...﴾ (17:23). Old age has its own dignity, but the weakness that comes with old age is also included in the word "kibar" (old age). And the phrase "indaka" (with you) indicates that in old age parents seek refuge with their children and also need support in their state of frailty.

﴿...say not to them "uff" and do not rebuke them...﴾ (17:23). This is the first stage of respect and courtesy toward parents: that no word be used by children toward parents that contains criticism, reproach, harshness or scolding, or anything that is disrespectful or falls within the category of bad manners.

﴿...but speak to them a noble word.﴾ (17:23). In terms of speech, this is an extremely high station: that parents be treated with the utmost respect.

"And lower to them the wing of humility out of mercy" (71:42 in the Urdu text's numbering; Qur'an 17:24). Here a very gentle and tender mode of expression has been adopted; within this mode, obedience, servitude and loyalty are given physical form. That is, lay yourself down and show such humility that it is as though "lowering" stood as an embodied bird, with wings, having spread its wings out.

"And say: My Lord, have mercy on them as they brought me up when I was small" (71:42 in the Urdu text's numbering; Qur'an 17:24). These are pleasant memories: memories of love, of childhood, and of the love of mother and father. But through this recollection it is being made clear to them that now these compassionate parents are in need of your compassion in the same way that you once were. The supplication is made because God's mercy and compassion are more important than human compassion, since the sphere of God's mercy and compassion is extremely vast, and only God can give the reward for the labour and hardship which they undertook for their children. It is possible for children to give their parents the mercy and compassion that they are entitled to only to a limited extent.

Hafiz Abu Bakr narrated with his chain of transmission, from Hadrat Buraydah, from his father, that a man was in the circumambulation (tawaf), carrying his mother and performing the tawaf with her. He asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "Have I thereby fulfilled her right?" He said: "No, not even a single breath (of hers)."

Since all of a person's impressions and actions are bound up with human outlook and come into being on the basis of that outlook, at the end of all these rulings all matters are returned to Allah, who knows intentions and also knows the intention behind states and actions.

Before further commands and instructions are given, and moral and legal rules are laid down, it is made known that Allah is aware of every word and every deed of a human being, and that His door is open. Every sinner can return and repent at any time. As long as a person has the capacity for reform within him, he can come back in repentance. The word "awwab" (one who turns back constantly to Allah, oft-returning in repentance) refers to the person who, when any fault comes from him, quickly returns to Allah and seeks repentance and forgiveness.

After parents, instructions are now given concerning close relatives, and along with relatives, the needy (masakin) and the traveller (musafir) are also included. Apart from close relatives, in the category of human relationships the needy and the traveller are the most deserving. Thus the sphere of good treatment and collective support has been extended to the whole of humanity.

Islam has established a right for relatives, the needy, and travellers over people's wealth, and this right can be fulfilled through spending (infaq) on these categories. Moreover, spending on these categories is not merely charity or kindness, but their right, which is incumbent upon the neck of every Muslim. Having made this right an obligation, Islam has linked it to the Islamic creed of tawhid and to Islamic worship and servitude, and thereby declared it to be an act of worship. This is a right and obligation from which the one charged with it can be cleared only upon its fulfilment. The one who spends in these categories is discharging his obligation, and on the other side, love will also arise between him and the one who benefits.

After this, the Qur'an prohibits tabdhir (extravagance, wasteful spending). What is tabdhir? Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them) used to define it as spending in a category where there is no right to spend. Mujahid says that if a person spends his entire wealth on the path of truth, it would still be tabdhir, and if someone spends even two kilograms without right, that is tabdhir.

Therefore, tabdhir does not relate to the quantity of spending, but to the category in which it is spent. The wasteful (mubadhdhirin) have been called brothers of the devils because they spend in falsehood, evil and disobedience. They are companions of the devil, and the devil is ungrateful to his Lord; He does not give thanks for the bounties of his Lord. And the brothers of the devil also do not give thanks for the bounties of Allah. The right of Allah's bounties is that they be spent in their proper place.

If a person does not have enough wealth to fulfil the rights of relatives, the needy and travellers, and he feels shame in facing them, then he should ask Allah to grant abundant provision to him and to them as well. He should also make a promise to these rightful people that when circumstances improve and he is able to do something, he will do it; he should make this promise and speak to them in a good and gentle manner. He should not display narrowness of heart or meanness, and he should not remain silent either, lest they feel distress in their hearts and interpret his silence in other ways, because speaking well and explaining gently will bring them reassurance.

Since in the previous verse tabdhir and extravagance were prohibited, in relation to that, moderation in spending is commanded here.
